display_title: Official Review of Paper2722 by Reviewer gduM

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper addresses the problem of local feature detection with a deep model
that outputs keypoints together with their characteristic orientation.

The model is made of a backbone that takes advantage of equivariant
convolutional layers (Weiler & Cesa 2019) to produce deep features invariant to
isometries in $\mathbb{R^2}$. These features are fed to two heads: the first one
produces a heatmap which local maxima are keypoint locations. The second head
generates an orientation histogram for each spatial location of the image.

The main contribution of the paper is the definition of a deep architecture
that learns keypoint's orientation in the form of an orientation histogram and the
associated histogram loss to train it.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

+ The choice of a histogram representation for the point's orientation is
  novel.

+ The model is trained in a self-supervised way with image pairs generated by
  synthetic transformation of a single image.

+ The model takes advantage of equivariant convolutional layers that are
  invariant to isometries in $\mathbb{Z}^2$. This infuses the keypoint with a
  theoretical property of rotation/symmetry and translation invariance, which
  is critical for keypoint detection. The model processes the image at multiple
  scales which grants the detection scale robustness too.

+ The experiments compare the proposed methods on the standard evaluation
  datasets for keypoint detection.

Weaknesses:

- Even though the writing allows for an intuitive understanding of the method,
  a non-negligible writing effort would help the reader (even an initiated one)
  understand the derivation details more smoothly. See below for a non-exhaustive
  list of improvements. 

- As mentioned in the paper, previous related works addressed the keypoint
  detection and orientation learning within the context of keypoint and
  description learning (e.g. (Yi et al.) (Ono et al.)). Even though the
  descriptor loss is backpropagated through the orientation layers, there is
  also an orientation-specific loss component that regresses the estimation
  orientation against a ground-truth one. Modulating the claim
  that 'Recently, existing learning methods [...] train the orientation by
  implicit way.' (in the intro) would better reflect that.
  
- Although novel, the histogram representation introduced in this paper is not
  compared against the orientation regression approaches (e.g. (Yi et al.) (Ono
  et al.)) so it is not possible to assess its performance advantage.  Running
  the released code of these methods on the evaluations datasets would allow
  the reader to better appreciate the contribution.

- Some technical claims would need to be reformulated (see list below).

Yi et al.: Lift: Learned invariant feature transform
Ono et al.: Lf-net: learning local features from images. 

Technical claims:
- 'several dense matching methods [...] find correspondences by correlation
  tensor': some of the cited methods do not use correlation tensors e.g. DTone,
  Dusmanu.
- 'dense matching [...] fail to find accurate matches': it would benefit the
  method to specify that this is because they can not detect keypoint at pixel
  accuracy, which is critical for visual applications, whereas the proposed
  method does. 
- 'Lowe [] gradient aggregation' -> 'gradient histogram'
- 'along with the ground-truth homography' suggests that a homography is
  learned by the network, which is not the case.
- 'then transforming the feature map by g' -> 'by $T_g'$ according to the paper
- when recalling the equivariant convolution, it would help the author to
  specify that $x$ is in $\mathbb{R}^2$ or $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and not an image.
  Also, what are $X$ and $Y$?
- The recall of group-equivariant convolutions is hard to grasp so it may be
  better to leave the reader to refer to the original paper if they need more
  details and save the space for additional experiment results.
- Although intuitive, adding the indices in equation 10 would help the reader
  understand the derivation details.
- Eq 11: the index j,k should be around (u,v) i.e. j=u-N/2 to j=u+N/2.
- '$m^{(i)}$ is non-maximal suppressed NxN patch' -> it is the softmax derived
  over the a spatial window of size NxN around (u,v)
- Eq12: when comparing the paper's notation with the original paper, it seems
  that $W_u=u$ and $W_v=v$.
- In the original paper $[\hat{x}^{(i)}, \hat{y}^{(i)}]$ are the coordinates of
  the maximum in the score map K in that window. Is the change to the 'weighted
  average index' a choice or an incorrect description?
- $\alpha^{(i)} = K\_{y^{(i)}, x^{(i)}; a} + T_g^{-1} K\_{y^{(i)}, x^{(i)}; b}$,
 should be $\alpha^{(i)} = K\_{y^{(i)}, x^{(i)}; a} + K\_{y^{(i)}, x^{(i)}; b}$
 since $K\_{y^{(i)}, x^{(i)}; b}$ is the real value that represents the
 importance of this location so it is incorrect to appply a transform $T_g^{-1}$ that
 operates over $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
- Eq 16: the notations are confusing. Is $\textbf{p}$ a pair of matching points
  or the whole set of matching points? The index $i$ is not introduced, neither
  $o_a$ and $o_b$ and $\delta$ is not used.
- AdaLAM is a match filtering method that uses both the orientation and the scale
  of the keypoints. How is the keypoint scale specified when evaluating on
  IMC21? 

Non-exhaustive suggested writing updates: a quick way to make these updates
would be entering the texts within a spell checker such as 'Grammarly'.
- 'correspondences to extract' -> 'by extracting'
- 'utilizes to assign' -> 'is used to assign'
- 'and following to' -> 'followed by'
- 'which is implemented by 1x1 group convolution': repetition
- 'are used to input' -> 'are used as input'
- 'for the given ground-truth rotation' -> 'with the'
- In the recall of the loss, it would be better not to recall the state-of-the
  art of keypoint detection but just describe the one that is used.
- 'index proposal': it is not clear for a random reader that the 'index
  proposal method' is the Barroso-Laguna loss.
- 'index kernel': not defined.
- 'generate randomly to transform': to reformulate

Misc suggestions:
- Fig3: the color orientation map is relevant but it would be even more
  informative there was also the bottom image on which would be applied
  $T_g^{-1} and $T'g' and draw it against the original one. This way, the
  reader could appreciate better the similarities between the orientations of
  the original image and the rotated one.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The main contribution of the paper is the self-supervised learning of the
keypoint's orientation through a novel representation (orientation histograms).
However, the lack of comparison against previous orientation representations
prevents the reader to appreciate the advantage of this representation.
Also there is significant margin for improvement in the writing (see
non-exhaustive suggestions above).
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2722 by Reviewer kzBH

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an architecture to detect keypoints invariant to rotation transforms. The architecture is based on extracting features with the rotation-equivariant layers of Weiler and Cesa. The extracted features are used to feed two branches: a keypoint detection and an orientation prediction network. While the error in the keypoint detection branch is computed by the window-based keypoint detection loss from Barroso-Laguna et al.’s work, the orientation error in the second branch is calculated by alignment the orientation histogram in the feature domain. The proposed detector was tested in two datasets, namely HPatches and IMC2021. The reported results showed that the new detector was superior in terms of MMA and repeatability score.
content.main_review:
I found the architecture designing, the strategy of pooling the channels and the groups differently, and the orientation alignment in the feature space to be sound and interesting. Other than that, its main components are built upon previous works, e.g., rotation-equivariant layers and keypoint detection loss. 

This reviewer thinks that the main weakness of this paper is the assessment, which is not well justified and does not sufficiently validate the proposed method.

First, the proposed architecture presents several design choices that are not well tested and motivated. More specifically, more details regarding the proposed methodology and an ablation analysis would significantly improve the paper and make the results more convincing. For instance, how is the performance of the detection without the orientation estimation branch? Is the orientation worse when removing the keypoint prediction branch? How does the multi-scale pyramid influence the final performance? Why use max-pooling in the group and 1D convolution in the channel tensors? How are the numbers with max pooling in both pooling operations? Are the numbers worse when measuring the rotation error in the image space instead of applying the histogram alignment in the feature space?

Second, the experimental results lack rotation and scale tests as done in Rublee et al., 2011 (Figures 7 and 8, Section 4.4). Since the paper proposes a rotation-equivariant keypoint detector, these experiments are strongly recommended. Moreover, it is not clear why the work of Yi et al., 2016 is not in the experiments. I understand that it only tries to estimate the orientation when the proposed work was designed to detect the keypoints and estimate the orientation. However, wouldn’t it be a good baseline to evaluate the quality of the orientation prediction branch? This reviewer also missed the LIFT detector/descriptor in the experiments. Since it is also a learned-based detector, it feels like a good baseline for the matching comparison.

Regarding the presentation and method description, some details could be included to improve the paper. 

1) In the paragraph detailing the implementation is stated that the input pairs share the weights. However, it is unclear which weights in the architecture. Are all weights shared or only the weights from the rotation-equivariant layers?
2) Please make clear that the rotation is in-plane rotation.
3) How many keypoints of each detector were used in the experiments? 
4) Please make clear why each detector and descriptor were used in the comparison. For example, why not ORB, Fast, Kaze, Freak, etc. There is no need to compare against all, but the selection criterion must be clear.
5) How was the repeatability computed? I.e., was used an elliptic region? What was the overlap error threshold used to consider two regions corresponding?

Some minor typos could be corrected to improve the overall quality of the paper:

1) Kindly consider rephrasing the following sentences for clarity: (i) “The rotation-equivariant representation utilizes to assign orientations to keypoints.” and (ii) “However, in general, a good keypoint means to be extracted a consistent location invariant to geometric or photometric image transformations”
2) convoluational layers = convolutional layers
3) keypoints invarint = keypoint invariant 
4) The diagram in Figure 1 must be revised. For instance, it lacks the interpolation step in the keypoint prediction branch.

At last, I recommend including some discussion about the limitations of the methodology.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea is reasonable, but the authors lack some experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model. Many technical components are adopted without strong motivation and/or experimental results to support the choice, which makes the overall conclusion much less convincing.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2722 by Reviewer d8xK

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a novel architecture and loss to train CNN-based keypoint detection method for the task of image matching. 
The main contributions are
1) Using group-equivariant convolutions to achieve rotation-equivariant keypoint detection.
2) Estimation of rotation-invariant orientations of these keypoints using alignment of histograms from the extracted rotation-equivariant keypoints.
The performance of the proposed rotation-equivariant keypoint is evaluated on several well-known image matching benchmarks with varying tasks and metrics, and shows improvement upon rotation-variant baselines.
content.main_review:
## Strengths
The paper is clearly written and technically sound. The method is well motivated, explained and polished. In terms of originality, to my best knowledge this is the first work that uses group-equivariant convolutions for rotation-equivariance in the specific task of image matching.

## Weaknesses
Although I mentioned in strengths about that this work is first to my knowledge to propose rotation-equivariance on keypoint detection, I cannot help but see the similarity between this work and GIFT [A], which proposed rotation-equivariant dense visual descriptors using similar techniques of group-equivariant convolutions and group pooling. It is completely fine in terms of originality to adapt a technique to a different task, as the details of implementation can be different, which is the case here. However, it is not ok to not even reference such related work in the paper at all and not compare with it as a baseline, especially when the ideas share a lot in common (e.g. the concept of “stacking” rotation-equivariant layers in Sec. 3.2 in this work v.s. that after Lemma 2 in Sec 3.2 of [A]). Unfortunately, since the biggest contribution of this paper is the rotation-equivariant detection as the losses used for training in later parts are from previous works, I believe the validity of this contribution is very weak when the most relevant method is not referenced and compared to.

For the results, even though GIFT is a descriptor method, I still think it can be used as a baseline for this work by mixing GIFT with rotation-invariant v.s. equivariant keypoints, as well as mixing the proposed method in this work with GIFT, LISRD [B] (which is another related work that is motivated by rotation invariance that this work fails to cite) v.s. other descriptors that are not rotation equivariant. This should still provide a lot of interesting insights and help strengthen the core contribution of this work.

Moreover, even without the comparison with GIFT, the results in Table 1 give mixed results. The proposed method improves only in number of matches in HPatches without the orientation estimation when compared with Key.Net, i.e. the group-equivariant convolutions alone does not really work for keypoint detection. However, adding the outlier filtering using the proposed orientation estimation causes significant drop in number of matches, i.e. the two proposed components do not work well together for this important benchmark. The results on IMC2021 in Table 2 is also not evaluated on common procedure, which usually reports results on 2k & 8k keypoints used; instead the results only significantly improve with 1k keypoints, which is not a commonly used metric. Well it is a merit that this method improved camera pose estimation in low compute, I think the lack of discussion on this observation is another weakness in the results section. Lastly, the qualitative results also do not give much information as there is no reference point of how a baseline method performs in the examples shown compared to the proposed method.

References:

[A]: Liu et al., GIFT: Learning Transformation-Invariant Dense Visual Descriptors via Group CNNs. In NeurIPS, 2019. 

[B]: Pautrat et al., Online Invariance Selection for Local Feature Descriptors. In ECCV, 2020.
content.summary_of_the_review: As mentioned in the main review, although there is no clear novelty or technical issues with this work, the failure to cite the most relevant baseline work is a major concern in my review. The proposed contributions also do not prove to work well together or consistently improve upon the benchmarks as mentioned above. Hence, I think this work needs major re-working in order to be accepted at a top-venue such as ICLR and I recommend **3: reject, not good enough**.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2722 by Reviewer 3XZ6

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work proposes a method for learning feature point detectors for visual correspondence.  

The key ideas/contributions are as following:

(a) use a rotation-equivariant feature extraction backbone [Cohen et al.].
(b) predict from the above features: 
     (i)  a rotation invariant keypoint location map (this is done as proposed in the "Index Proposal Layer" of [Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019], and 
     (ii) a rotation equivariant "orientation" map (which associates each location in the visual feature map with a local orientation). This is achieved by aligning the orientation in a manner similar to the RiRoI align method "ReDet" of [Han et al., 2021]. A cross-entropy loss is used to align these orientation "histograms".
(c) experimental comparison against two detectors -- SIFT and Key.Net [Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019] is performed (with various feature extractors) on the HPatches and IMC2021 benchmarks. The proposed method is shown to outperform both methods on the two datasets.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
(i) a novel use of rotation-equivariant backbone for feature-point detection. Prior work of  [Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019] which proposed the "Index Proposal Layer" employed in this work as well, did not use rotation-equivariant features.
(ii) a novel use of the "RiRoI" of ReDet [Han et al. 2021] for aligning orientation "histograms".
(iii) the method is trained in a self-supervised manner, which does not limit the scale of supervision (this is also common in prior work in this area, nonetheless a positive aspect).
(iv) the proposed method is demonstrated to outperform prior work (both SIFT and Key.Net).


Weaknesses:
(i) the key weakness of this work is that it is an amalgamation of pre-existing works, namely -- rotation-equivariant feature-extractors [Cohen et al.], RiRoI for orientation alignment of ReDet [Han et al., 21], and the Index Proposal Layer [Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019].  In fact, ReDet also uses a rotation equivariant network with appropriate orientation alignment (RiRoI) but for (aerial) object detection.  Hence, overall the technical novelty of this work is limited.

(ii) the proposed method lags behind key.net without filtering, and requires a filtering stage to surpass it (albeit by only a small margin on HPatches). The results with the baseline (key.net) + filtering are not presented for fair comparison.

(iii) The comparisons are limited to SIFT and Key.Net. More recent methods like LLF [Suwanwimolkul et al.] outperform key.net (admittedly marginally). Comparisons to LLF should be included for completeness.
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the relatively incremental nature of technical contribution and the requirement of a filtering stage (please see the details above), I am inclined to reserve my recommendation for this work. The authors are encouraged to address the points highlighted (esp. wrt requiring a filtering stage, and comparisons w/o it) to strengthen their experiments.
